design_detail: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR; protocol preregistered on the Open Science Framework) of empirical studies of oral nicotine pouches, an update of the authors' 2024 review. MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO trial register were searched on 30 September 2025 (the first three from 2023 onward), English and German full texts. 481 titles and abstracts were screened by four reviewers independently and 181 full texts by two; 73 new studies were included (12 industry-funded), 135 across both reviews. Data were extracted in duplicate and reported in tables and narrative under five domains: use patterns, beliefs and perceptions, product characteristics, toxicity, and marketing and sales, with findings split by industry and non-industry funding. By the authors' own statement there was no risk-of-bias assessment and no statistical synthesis. The schema has no scoping-review design; 'systematic-review' is used because the search and selection are systematic.
can_establish: What surveys reported about how many people used pouches (US youth and adults to 2024, other countries to 2024) and who reported use; what laboratory analyses reported about pouch contents; what short trials reported about nicotine uptake, subjective ratings and cigarettes smoked; how few studies measure health outcomes; and how much of the literature is industry-funded.
cannot_establish: That pouches are less harmful than cigarettes or snus in the people who use them (there are no studies of disease or death, and the short measures of blood pressure and biomarkers are mixed); long-term effects (none measured); the certainty or quality of any finding (no appraisal); whether pouches help people stop smoking (trials of up to 6 months show fewer cigarettes and little quitting); how many people who never smoked take up pouches (prevalence among never-smokers is not given in the text); or comparability of prevalence between countries (sampling frames are not tabulated in the main text).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Six sources searched on 30 September 2025; MEDLINE, EMBASE and Web of Science limited to 2023 onward (the first review's search ended January 2024), the three trial sources from inception; references of eligible papers searched by one reviewer; only the PubMed strategy is published (Supplementary File S1, not read) (Materials and methods › Search strategy, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed empirical studies of oral nicotine pouches within the five domains, English or German. Excluded: pouches without nicotine, studies of several oral nicotine products without pouch-specific results, literature reviews, editorials, case reports, commentaries, letters and conference papers. The criteria are given by reference to the first review (Materials and methods › Eligibility, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Mostly US studies; others from the UK, Germany, Switzerland, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Poland, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Canada and Australia. Youth and adult surveys are reported separately (Results › Use patterns of ONPs, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Peer-reviewed papers in English or German only; no grey literature. The authors say the review's broad inclusion criteria allowed no appraisal and that associations with current use rest on generally small samples (Discussion, 9th paragraph). Prevalence figures mix national surveys with other samples (for example adult college students, online panels) without the main text saying which is which. The paper lists one pharmacokinetic and subjective-ratings crossover study (its reference 61) under non-industry-funded studies in one section and under industry-funded studies in another.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. Primary studies: self-reported lifetime use (ever) and current use (past 30 days, or every day or some days), measured product content, plasma nicotine in clinical crossover trials, urinary or blood biomarkers, and Nielsen retail sales (Materials and methods › Data synthesis, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Measured product content cited from primary analyses: total nicotine 1.41 to 8.11 mg per pouch in 70 US tobacco-free products; 6.4 (SD 3.5) mg per pouch against 12.3 (SD 8.2) mg in tobacco-based pouches in a second analysis of 50 products; 2.20 to 56 mg per pouch in 31 products sold in Germany; freebase share 63.4% against 47.2% for tobacco-based pouches (Results › Product characteristics › Nicotine content and release from pouches). Trials used single uses of 20 to 60 minutes up to 6 months. Route: oral.
exposure.polysubstance: Dual use is a main result, not a nuisance: most US youth reporting current pouch use in the Monitoring the Future survey also reported vaping, and use is concentrated among people who currently or formerly smoked or vaped (Results › Use patterns › US prevalence estimates, 1st paragraph; Demographic characteristics, 3rd paragraph). Surveys therefore cannot attribute outcomes to pouches alone.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable at review level; the pharmacokinetic trials enrolled people who smoke or use smokeless tobacco daily.

comparison.controls: Varies by primary study: continued smoking, nicotine gum, e-cigarettes, snus or moist snuff, cigarettes within the same session, or none in surveys.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not assessed at review level; many trials enrolled people who smoked daily without intent to quit.

outcomes.instruments: Survey prevalence (PATH, National Youth Tobacco Survey, Monitoring the Future, TUS-CPS and others), measured content, pharmacokinetic maxima and areas under the curve, subjective ratings, cytotoxicity assays, biomarkers, cigarettes per day and quit rates in trials, and sales units and revenue.
outcomes.validity_norms: No risk-of-bias assessment. The review separates findings by industry and non-industry funding instead.
outcomes.operationalization: Prevalence is reported as lifetime (ever) and current use with each survey's own definition (Supplementary Table S2, not read). Harm is not operationalised; there are no disease outcomes.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening and extraction by two or four reviewers working independently.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled effect sizes. Reported ranges: US youth 2024, current use 1.8% (National Youth Tobacco Survey, middle and high school) and 2.6% (Monitoring the Future, grades 10 and 12), lifetime 3.5% and 5.4%; US adults 2022 to 2023, current use 0.4% (TUS-CPS) to 0.8% (PATH), lifetime 2.7% to 3.3%; other countries, lifetime use from 3.3% (British youth 2024) to 27% (Canadian college students 2024) and current use from 0.4% (adults in England 2023) to 19% (Australia 2023). Sales: 327 million units (July 2021) to 1,046 million (May 2024). Trials: cigarettes per day fell by nearly half among people assigned to pouches in an 8-week three-arm trial of 33 daily smokers on low incomes (one switched completely, three stopped using pouches), both strengths cut cigarettes in a 4-week trial of 30 (two quit, both on the stronger pouch), and by over 90% in a 6-month industry-funded trial of 100; nicotine uptake from pouches ranged from below to above that from a cigarette by strength and brand.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Preregistered protocol on the Open Science Framework (cited as reference 11); no deviation is described; the registration was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessed. The review does not appraise the primary studies and reports funders for them.
analysis.power: Not assessed; the authors say associations with current pouch use should be interpreted with caution because of generally small samples.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Surveys show low but rising use in the US (adult current use under 1% in 2022 to 2023; youth current use 1.8% to 2.6% in 2024, more than doubling in three years), higher use in men, young adults and people who smoke, vape or use smokeless tobacco, and much higher figures in some other countries and samples. Nicotine uptake varies widely by strength and brand and can exceed or fall short of a cigarette's. Trials last 4 weeks to 6 months and show fewer cigarettes smoked with little complete switching. Evidence on toxicity is laboratory content analysis, cell assays (several industry-funded) and a few biomarker studies with mixed results. No study follows disease.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract: nicotine uptake from pouches of 6 mg or more 'typically exceeds' that from cigarettes; pouches are 'considerably less toxic than cigarettes'; trials 'suggest' pouches can reduce smoking. Discussion: independent and industry-funded trials found that pouch use for up to 6 months 'significantly decreased' cigarette and smokeless tobacco consumption; the pouches 'may be a less hazardous alternative to traditional tobacco' but are 'not risk-free'. Gaps: (1) the Results show a 6 mg pouch with lower peak and total nicotine than a cigarette in the independent German study, and 4 mg and 8 mg pouches below a cigarette in an industry series, while the Discussion moves the threshold to 8 mg and says 'often exceeds'; (2) 'considerably less toxic' rests on content and cell assays, a small biomarker comparison in which nicotine metabolites were comparable to those of people who smoke, and no reduction of tobacco-specific nitrosamines in the 4-week trial of dual use; (3) the Discussion says 'significantly decreased' for trials whose Results give no tests, the only 6-month trial being industry-funded.

timeline.event: The authors' first scoping review of oral nicotine pouches (search to January 2024; doi 10.1093/ntr/ntae131), which this review updates; it concluded that most evidence came from industry-funded studies.
Independent laboratory measurement of nicotine and tobacco-specific nitrosamines across pouch brands, one of the content analyses of the kind this review summarises.
Systematic review of the health effects of snus and tobacco-free pouches; it finds 15 human studies of pouches, none longer than 6 months.

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent map of the pouch literature in this batch, and the main source for who uses pouches and how much. It is a summary of other studies, so none of its findings is an independent replication of another; its strength is the split by funder and the explicit statement that health effects are understudied.

funding.funder: Grant 2U54CA229974 from the US National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute, and the Food and Drug Administration; the paper says the funders had no input on the protocol, interpretation or publication, as printed.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: one author (Goniewicz) received a research grant from Pfizer, served on a scientific advisory board to Johnson & Johnson and consulted for Kenvue 'outside of this work', and has consulted for the US Food and Drug Administration, the World Health Organization, the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids and the Polish Medical Research Agency; another (Hartmann-Boyce) has consulted for Truth Initiative. The paper does not say whether the other five authors have none.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at Georgetown University's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center, the University of Michigan, the University of Massachusetts Amherst, Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, Rutgers Cancer Institute and the BC Cancer Research Institute. No tobacco-industry funding or tie is declared. Industry-funded primary studies (British American Tobacco, Altria, Japan Tobacco International) are identified in the text and set beside the others.

what_would_settle_it: Independent, registered cohorts and trials of people who use pouches alone, including people who never smoked, followed for years, with measured nicotine intake, biomarkers of exposure and harm and disease outcomes, reported beside people who smoke, people who use snus and people who use no nicotine; national surveys that record never-smoker status, product type (tobacco-free or tobacco-based) and sampling frame; and a quality appraisal of the laboratory and trial literature that is split by funder.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: A scoping review organised by five outcome domains, not by question components; population, comparator and outcomes are not set out in this paper, which defers to the first review's eligibility criteria.
A preregistered protocol on the Open Science Framework is cited; no deviations are described and the registration was not read. The widening of the search to three trial registers is stated.
All empirical designs were eligible ('broad inclusion criteria') with no reason given for each.

Six sources including three trial registers, a stated date and a flow chart, but peer-reviewed English or German papers only without a stated reason, the three main databases limited to 2023 onward (to avoid overlap with the first review), references checked by one reviewer, and no experts or grey literature. Judged 'no' on the project's reading of item 4 (decision p-amstar2-item4). Only the PubMed strategy is published, in a supplement not read.
Four reviewers screened titles and abstracts independently and two screened full texts independently; disagreements were settled by consensus.
Two reviewers extracted independently with a standardized tool and compared entries.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Counts only (181 read in full, 73 new studies kept); no list of the excluded studies is referenced in the page text; the flow chart (an image) was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The text gives design, size, duration, product and funder for many studies; characteristics of all 135 studies are in Supplementary Table S1, not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: None was done, by the authors' statement (Discussion, 9th paragraph).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Each section separates industry-funded studies from the rest and names the funders; 12 of the 73 new studies were industry-funded. One crossover study (reference 61) is placed in both groups.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: No assessment was made to account for; the Discussion weighs funder and sample size in passing ('mainly industry-funded', 'low sample sizes').

The Discussion attributes differences to survey definitions, populations and product features (nicotine content, release, freebase share) and says a conclusion for the whole product category cannot be made.
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Grant and funder role stated; interests of two authors listed; the paper does not say whether the other authors have none.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 rates four critical items 'no' (search, list of excluded studies, risk-of-bias assessment, risk of bias in interpretation) and the protocol only partly, so the review is critically low confidence as an accurate and comprehensive summary of quality-appraised studies. AMSTAR 2 was written for reviews that appraise and combine evidence, which a scoping review does not set out to do, so the rating chiefly states what this review cannot supply (quality-graded conclusions). Its search and screening are otherwise careful (preregistered, duplicate screening and extraction, trial registers added, funders named and findings split by funding). It may be cited for the map it draws: survey prevalence and who reports use, the counts and designs of pouch studies, measured contents, the range of nicotine uptake, how long the trials ran, and which findings are industry-funded; each figure is second-hand from named primary studies. It may not be cited for a quality-weighted judgment, for harm or benefit of pouches, for a comparison with smoking or snus, or for the statement that nicotine uptake from pouches of 6 mg or more typically exceeds that from cigarettes.

key_findings.finding: Scope: 481 titles and abstracts screened, 181 full texts, 73 new studies (12 industry-funded), 135 across both reviews; six sources searched to 30 September 2025; English and German; no risk-of-bias assessment and no statistical synthesis; findings are split by industry and non-industry funding.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Materials and methods, 1st paragraph; Search strategy, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 9th paragraph

key_findings.finding: US youth: in PATH (ages 12 to 17, 2022 to 2023) lifetime pouch use was 0.9% and current use 0.2%; in the National Youth Tobacco Survey (middle and high school) lifetime use rose from 1.9% to 3.5% and current use from 0.8% to 1.8% between 2021 and 2024; in Monitoring the Future (grades 10 and 12) lifetime use rose from 3% to 5.4% and current use from 1.3% to 2.6% between 2023 and 2024, with most reporting dual use with e-cigarettes. Among adolescents currently using pouches in 2024, 29% reported frequent use and 22% daily use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Use patterns of ONPs › US prevalence estimates, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: US adults 2022 to 2023: PATH lifetime pouch use 3.3% and current use 0.8%; TUS-CPS lifetime use 2.7% and current use 0.4%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Use patterns of ONPs › US prevalence estimates, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other countries, lifetime (current) use: British youth 2024 3.3% (1.2%); Quebec adolescents 2024 3.7% (2.6%); Australia 2023 26% (19%) among youth and adults; Pakistan 2022 17.2% (9.4%) among youth and adults; Finland 2022 14.4% (3.7%) among youth and adults and 2023 17.2% (7.2%) among youth; adults in the UK 2024 13%, Great Britain 5.4% (1%), Poland 2024 9.2% (4.3%), Canadian college students 2024 27% (12%); Saudi Arabia lifetime use 14.2% in the general population and 21.2% among people with a tobacco history; Sweden 1.4% and Denmark 0.8% current use in 2019.
key_findings.locator: Results › Use patterns of ONPs › Prevalence estimates in other countries, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Sampling frames are not given in the main text; the Swedish and Danish figures come from a British American Tobacco-funded survey (reference 15).

key_findings.finding: Who reports use: among adolescents and adults, higher odds of lifetime or current pouch use in males, younger ages, and people who currently or formerly smoked, vaped or used smokeless tobacco; in US surveys also non-Hispanic whites; education mixed; household income not associated.
key_findings.locator: Results › Use patterns of ONPs › Demographic characteristics, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Pouches and other nicotine use: in an 8-week three-arm trial of 33 daily smokers on low incomes, those assigned to pouches cut cigarettes per day by nearly half, one person switched completely and three stopped using pouches; in a 4-week trial of 30, both 3 mg and 6 mg strengths cut cigarettes and two people on 6 mg stopped smoking; in a 6-month industry-funded trial of 100, cigarettes per day fell by over 90%; in a US cross-sectional study, quitting cigarettes was associated with daily pouch use; 73% of Pakistani adults currently using pouches also smoked; 41% of Saudi adults with a tobacco history who tried pouches reported quitting.
key_findings.locator: Results › Impact on other tobacco/nicotine product use, 1st paragraph; Non-industry-funded studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nicotine uptake: in an independent German crossover study of adults who smoked daily, a 30 mg pouch gave the highest peak and total nicotine over 4 hours, then a cigarette, then 20 mg and 6 mg pouches (time to peak 5 minutes for the cigarette, 20 minutes for the 6 mg pouch); in adults who used smokeless tobacco daily, 8 mg pouches delivered comparable or more nicotine than smokeless tobacco after 30 minutes of use; in industry-funded series, 4 mg and 8 mg pouches gave lower peak and total nicotine than a cigarette and 12 mg and 8 mg 'mini' pouches comparable or higher, with time to peak 35 to 40 minutes against 5 to 7 for a cigarette; in adults who used Swedish snus, peak and 60-minute nicotine from 6, 9 and 11.2 mg pouches were higher than from 11.2 mg snus (twice as high for the 11.2 mg pouch), and pouches delivered nicotine slightly faster than snus and nicotine gum. Four of eight new pharmacokinetic trials were industry-funded (British American Tobacco, Japan Tobacco International).
key_findings.locator: Results › Product characteristics › Pharmacokinetics; Non-industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph; Industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Measured content: a US analysis of 70 tobacco-free products found 1.41 to 8.11 mg total nicotine per pouch; a second analysis of 50 pouches found 6.4 (SD 3.5) mg against 12.3 (SD 8.2) mg in tobacco-based pouches with a higher freebase share (63.4% against 47.2%); 31 pouches sold in Germany held 2.20 to 56 mg; measured nicotine was generally equal to or below the label. Elemental analysis of six pouches found aluminium, barium, chromium, copper, iron, manganese, strontium, titanium and others (not quantified); artificial sweeteners were present at 0.3 to 1.2 mg per pouch, even in unflavoured products.
key_findings.locator: Results › Product characteristics › Nicotine content and release from pouches, 1st paragraph; Toxicity › Chemical content, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Toxicity in cells: an independent assay found more pro-inflammatory cytokines than a pure nicotine solution; a British American Tobacco-funded assay found seven of eight own-brand pouches non-cytotoxic, non-mutagenic and non-genotoxic and cigarettes positive in all three tests, with one 8 mg spice-flavoured pouch cytotoxic and genotoxic at high concentrations; an Altria-funded analysis found that two of seven nicotine degradants and impurities exceeded the toxicity of nicotine itself.
key_findings.locator: Results › Toxicity › In vitro toxicity › Non-industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph; Industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers and physiology in people: in PATH data (small sample), nicotine metabolites in people who used only pouches were higher than in people who used only e-cigarettes and comparable to people who smoked; minor tobacco alkaloids, cadmium and uranium were lower than in people who smoked and similar to vapers; lead was lower than in people who smoked or vaped; in the 4-week trial, dual use with pouches did not lower tobacco-specific nitrosamines; 20-minute use of 20 mg and 30 mg pouches raised systolic pressure and arterial stiffness comparably to a cigarette; an Altria-funded trial found less gingivitis and staining at 24 weeks after switching.

Sales and marketing: Nielsen data (excluding online and specialty shops) show US pouch sales rising from 327 million units in July 2021 to 1,046 million in May 2024 and revenue from US$61 million to US$232 million, with four brands holding 99.8%; exposure to marketing was associated with use and appeal in youth and adults.
key_findings.locator: Results › Marketing and sales › Market share and sales data, 1st paragraph; ONP advertising, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Authors' reading: health effects of pouches 'remain largely understudied'; the evidence of short-term benefit from switching is 'limited, mainly industry-funded'; co-use with other products is high and the effect on smoking cessation unclear; pouches 'may be a less hazardous alternative to traditional tobacco' but 'are not risk-free'.
key_findings.note: Short quotations are the authors' wording.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says nicotine uptake from pouches of 6 mg or more typically exceeds that from cigarettes. In the Results, a 6 mg pouch gave lower peak and total nicotine than a cigarette in the independent German study, and 4 mg and 8 mg pouches were below a cigarette in an industry series; the Discussion says 6 mg or more in the first review and 8 mg or more in the update 'often exceeds'.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results › Product characteristics › Pharmacokinetics; Discussion, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Uptake relative to a cigarette depends on strength, brand and study; the abstract sentence cannot be cited as it stands.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says trials of up to 6 months, independent and industry-funded, 'significantly decreased' cigarette and smokeless tobacco use. The Results give no tests for the independent trials (n = 33, 8 weeks; n = 30, 4 weeks) and the only 6-month trial (n = 100) is industry-funded.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Results › Impact on other tobacco/nicotine product use
reporting_issues.consequence: The word 'significantly' is not supported by the Results text; use the Results figures.

reporting_issues.issue: One crossover study (reference 61, a 30-minute five-product study in people who use snus) is listed under non-industry-funded studies for subjective ratings and under industry-funded studies for pharmacokinetics; the funder is not named.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Product characteristics › Subjective ratings › Non-industry-funded studies, 2nd paragraph; Pharmacokinetics › Industry-funded studies, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of 12 industry-funded studies cannot be reproduced from the text; the funder of this study is unresolved.

reporting_issues.issue: The 6-month 'parallel-group trial of 100' with over 90% fewer cigarettes and the 'Altria-funded' 24-week trial of gingivitis are both cited to reference 17 (an oral-health trial of switching to on! pouches); the snus-and-pouch review in this batch lists that trial with 155 participants and 44 men and 56 women.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Impact on other tobacco/nicotine product use › Industry-funded studies; Toxicity › Human studies; compare sc_kopa_stojak_2026
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the trial is printed as 100 here and 155 there; its funder is stated here (Altria) but not in the other review.

reporting_issues.issue: Prevalence figures come from national surveys and from other samples in one running list (for example Australia 26% lifetime, Canadian college students 27%, against 3.3% of US adults); the text does not say which are probability samples.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Use patterns › Prevalence estimates in other countries
reporting_issues.consequence: Cross-country comparison of prevalence from this list is not safe.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 11, the protocol, carries the first review's journal volume and page numbers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Clerical; the protocol could not be located from the printed reference.
